title: Feedback That Changes What People Do

audience.who: corporate employees who give feedback to peers or to people they lead
audience.knows: that feedback matters, and usually gives it as general praise, general criticism or a hint
audience.cares_about: getting a colleague to actually do something differently next time without hurting the working relationship

outcome: After watching, a viewer can take a vague comment they were about to give and turn it into feedback that names one observed behaviour, the effect it had, and one concrete thing to try next time.
through_line: Feedback that only moves feelings leaves behaviour where it was; saying what someone did, what it caused and what to try next gives them something they can actually change.

arc_plan.what: A team lead tells a colleague 'great job, maybe tighten things up a bit' after a project update; the colleague smiles, feels fine, and runs the next update exactly the same way.
The viewer will leave able to turn that kind of comment into feedback the colleague can act on, using the same two people and the same update.
Connect the viewer's own memory of hearing a kind but vague comment to why the opening comment changed nothing: it gave a feeling, not a target.

Rework the same comment in three visible additions: the specific behaviour that was observed, the effect it had on others or the work, then one concrete next step agreed together. The one comment changes as each part is added.
A different small workplace moment with a vague comment; the viewer picks which of two rewrites names behaviour, effect and next step.
Invite the viewer to pick one piece of feedback they owe someone this week and rebuild it the same way before they say it.
Return to the same colleague and the next project update, now after the reworked feedback, and show the update run differently.

must_cover.what: Why vague or purely feelings-based feedback rarely changes what someone does
Describing specific observed behaviour rather than judging character or personality
Naming the effect the behaviour had on others or on the work
Ending with a concrete, forward-looking next step, ideally agreed in conversation
Giving feedback soon after the moment it is about

must_avoid: Statistics or research figures without a source
Invented sayings presented as real research
Opening with a textbook meaning of the word feedback or an agenda
A trainer-with-a-checklist tone or talking down to the viewer
Presenting one named feedback model as the only correct one
Implying positive feedback is bad; the point is specificity, not tone
example_posture: One running example: a team lead and one colleague whose project updates run long and bury the key decision. Realistic, low drama, the same two people throughout; the check uses a different small moment so it tests the skill, not memory.
visual_direction: Story-cartoon look: two people in a recognisable workplace moment, the one comment shown as something that visibly gains parts as each piece is added, a before and after of the same update, and a glimpse of the next update going differently. One loud thing at a time, the narrator as an occasional presenter, not a talking head.
voice_note: Mentor: a warm, experienced colleague who has given vague feedback too and says so; direct, unhurried, never a lecturer.
open_questions: Whether the organisation already uses a named feedback model is unknown; the lesson stays model-neutral.
No preference was given for how much on-screen presenter time is wanted beyond the 10 percent ceiling.

inferred: the running example of a team lead and a colleague's long project updates
the behaviour, effect, next step build
giving feedback soon after the moment as a must_cover item
